source: Dinh, Ding, Qu, Thilakarathna (2026) Memory Retrieval in Transformers: Insights from the Encoding Specificity Principle [Exp 1: attention swapping]
finding: Maps attention to cue-based retrieval: query = retrieval context, key = trace index, value = content. Swapping projections between factual and counterfactual prompts (same token length) gives forgetting-like or hallucination-like failures. Swapping K alone hurts recall but does not make the model say the counterfactual. Swapping V alone makes it answer the counterfactual. Swapping K and V makes it hallucinate on every prompt.
numbers: Counterfactual dataset (Meng et al. 2022). Seven open models (Llama 2 7b/13b, Llama 3.1 8b, Olmo 2 13b, Qwen 2.5 14b, Phi-4, GPT-NeoX 20b). V swap: counterfactual answers 50% (Olmo 2) to 90% (Qwen 2.5). K+V swap: 100% counterfactual in all models. K swap: factual accuracy about 30-40%. Swap applied to the prompt only, not to generated tokens.
quote: swapping V alone induces LLMs to hallucinate and answer as if they were prompted
limits: Swap only at prompt time; the K-only result is read as retrieval failure but could have other causes. Counterfactual prompts are short fact completions, not agent memory. No human comparison and no cue-mismatch manipulation. Arxiv preprint, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: In a model, a wrong key (cue) with an intact value gives silent forgetting; a wrong value gives confident wrong content. So a missed lesson and a misleading lesson are different failure modes and need different checks.

source: Dinh, Ding, Qu, Thilakarathna (2026) Memory Retrieval in Transformers: Insights from the Encoding Specificity Principle [Exp 2: K perturbation of keywords]
finding: Hypothesis: the cues are salient keywords. Zeroing the key projection of identified keywords in top attention heads lowers verbatim recall of memorized book passages more than zeroing random words. Each book has one dominant layer-head-dimension unit, consistent across books. Olmo 2 with all heads perturbed: recall fell sharply for keywords but barely for random words.
numbers: Project Gutenberg books; 512-token input, 40-token output windows kept only when ROUGE-L recall = 1. 20 keywords per method. Compared GPT-4o-chosen keywords, LXT relevance keywords, and their key-projection method. Keywords beat random for every model except Llama 2 7b/13b, where the three keyword sets were close to random on ROUGE-L recall. LXT cut recall most but also damaged MAUVE and repetition. Per-model effect sizes are only in radar plots, not tables.
limits: Narrow: verbatim recall of public-domain books. Keyword lists came from GPT-4o and a heuristic. Authors admit neuron and keyword counts are arbitrary and multi-word terms ('white rabbit') are split. The authors blame the small Llama 2 vocabulary (32,000 vs 128,256 for Llama 3.1) for the null; this is untested.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that in-model retrieval runs on a few content words. A lesson key should carry the distinctive nouns and terms that will be in the future query, not generic words.

source: Stern and Nadel (2026) Drawing on Memory: Dual-Trace Encoding Improves Cross-Session Recall in LLM Agents
finding: An agent stores each fact plus a concrete 'scene' (who, where, when it was learned). Compared with a fact-only store of the same format and coverage, accuracy rose 20 points on LongMemEval-S. The authors frame this as encoding specificity: extra encoded context gives extra retrieval paths.
numbers: 99 paired questions, Claude Sonnet as agent, GPT-4o judge. Dual-trace 73.7% vs fact-only 53.5%, +20.2 pp, 95% CI [+12.1, +29.3], bootstrap p<0.0001. McNemar: 22 questions only dual-trace right, 2 only fact-only right, chi2=15.04. Session coverage 54.8% vs 57.4%. Vanilla Letta without protocol: 20.0%, all from abstention credit.
limits: One run, one benchmark, one agent model. The paper itself lists an encoding/retrieval confound: the scene is also reconstructed at retrieval, so the gain cannot be assigned to encoding alone. Elaborative generation (drawing effect) is an equally good explanation as encoding specificity. Preprint, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Best direct test of 'write the circumstances with the lesson' in an agent loop. Cheap to copy: store problem class, trigger and situation next to each lesson.

source: Stern and Nadel (2026) Dual-trace per-category results
finding: The scene benefit appears only where several traces must be told apart or ordered. No gain on single-session facts, large gains on temporal, update and multi-session questions. This matches the human pattern that extra cues help when many similar traces compete.
numbers: n=20 per category. Single-session 75% vs 75% (p=0.657). Multi-session 50 vs 20 (+30, p=0.001). Knowledge-update 80 vs 55 (+25, p=0.003). Temporal 65 vs 25 (+40, p=0.002). Abstention 100 vs 95 (p=0.351). Of 22 questions won only by dual-trace: 9 temporal, 6 multi-session, 5 update, 1 single, 1 abstention.
quote: Scene traces produce no gain on single-session fact retrieval
limits: Category CIs are wide (e.g. single-session CI [55,90]). The null on single-session is explained after the fact. Bootstrap assumes independent questions.
agent_relevance: Do not expect richer keys to help when only one lesson fits. Expect help when many lessons look alike. Measure by number of look-alike candidates.

source: Stern and Nadel (2026) Dual-trace development path and coverage effect
finding: Before the scene trace, better coverage and cleaner format moved accuracy only a little. Adding the scene was the big step. Early conditions with a broken trigger or low coverage scored 38-48%.
numbers: Conditions C1 40.4, C2 38.4, C3 47.5, C4 47.5, C5-FS (file-system index added) 48.5, C7 fact-only high coverage 53.5, C6 dual-trace 73.7. Authors call the C4-to-C7 step a +6 pp coverage gain. About 78% of LongMemEval-S sessions were routed to DROP (no personal information).
limits: The conditions were developed in sequence by the authors, so they are not independent arms. Only C6 vs C7 is a controlled pair.
agent_relevance: A lesson store with poor keys loses a lot even if coverage is high. Spend effort on key content before storing more.

source: Guo, Wu, Yiu (2026) The Interference Gap: Comparing Retrieval Bounds in Human Memory and RAG Systems [fan effect]
finding: Fits the same log-decline law to humans and retrievers: accuracy falls with the number of items sharing a cue (fan). Dense passage retrieval loses accuracy faster than humans; hippocampus-inspired HippoRAG sits near humans.
numbers: Humans N=112 (Prolific, 8 of 120 excluded): 91.2% at fan 1, 82.4% at fan 2, 71.8% at fan 4; Cohen's d=1.12 [0.89,1.35]; interference slope 0.41 [0.35,0.47]. Dense passage retrieval (DPR) 94.1->76.3->58.2->44.7% over fan 1,2,4,8; slope 0.67. ColBERTv2 0.53. HippoRAG 0.44. Parameter recovery r>=.93. Log form preferred to power law (BIC diff 15.7-23.1).
limits: Person-location sentences only. Humans tested at fan 1,2,4; fan 8 is simulated for RAG only. Not pre-registered. Old retrievers (DPR, ColBERTv2); newer embedders not tested. Recent unreviewed preprint; human data not independently verified.
agent_relevance: Many similar lessons under one cue is the main failure risk, not forgetting. Keep keys distinct, keep the store small per class, or index by more than one cue.

source: Guo, Wu, Yiu (2026) The Interference Gap: Comparing Retrieval Bounds in Human Memory and RAG Systems [serial position and mechanisms]
finding: Humans show recency, DPR shows primacy. The paper names encoding specificity as one of three mechanisms that could explain why humans resist interference, but says its data cannot separate it from temporal context binding or retrieval gating.
numbers: Serial position ratio (recency/primacy) humans 1.43, DPR 0.52, HippoRAG 0.89 [0.74,1.04]. DPR accuracy at position 1/10/20: 89.2/61.4/68.3%. HippoRAG 86.4/68.9/78.1%. System x position F(4,536)=8.73, p<.001.
limits: Mechanism claims are speculation by the authors ('convergence is not identification'). Six falsifiable predictions are listed, none tested here.
agent_relevance: Do not claim a retriever is doing encoding specificity on the basis of this paper. Treat it as a measurement frame: compare lesson retrieval with a fan curve from our own logs.

source: Wu et al. (2025) LongMemEval: Benchmarking Chat Assistants on Long-Term Interactive Memory [key design]
finding: Indexing a memory by its own text plus extracted facts (key = value + fact) beats indexing by the text alone, while indexing by the condensed form alone does not. This is a cue-widening result: keep the original cues and add new ones.
numbers: LongMemEval-M (500 sessions, about 1.5M tokens). Value=round: Recall@5 0.582 (K=V), 0.530 (K=fact), 0.282 (keyphrase), 0.644 (V+fact). Value=session: Recall@10 0.783 (K=V) vs 0.862 (V+fact). Averages: +9.4% recall@k and +5.4% final QA accuracy across GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 70B and 8B readers. GPT-4o QA top-10, round value: 0.670 (K=V) vs 0.720 (V+fact).
quote: using these condensed forms alone does not enhance the memory recall performance
limits: The authors do not frame it as encoding specificity. Merging at index time beat merging ranks at retrieval time (Appendix E.3). Gains are on one benchmark with a fixed retriever family.
agent_relevance: Store lessons under original wording plus generated cues (problem class, symptom, fix). Do not replace the original wording with a summary.

source: Wu et al. (2025) LongMemEval [time-aware query expansion and granularity]
finding: Adding a time cue on the query side helps when the question is about time. Splitting sessions into rounds helps the reader. A strong model is needed to turn the question into a time range.
numbers: Time-aware expansion raised recall by 11.3% on average with round values and 6.8% with session values. Temporal subset, session value, K=V+fact: Recall@10 0.721 -> 0.797 with GPT-4o expansion; with Llama 3.1 8B expansion 0.711 (no real gain). Round value K=V+fact Recall@10 0.550 -> 0.722 with GPT-4o.
limits: Gains depend on the strength of the model that rewrites the query. Benchmark conversations are synthetic with injected evidence sessions.
agent_relevance: Rewriting the query into the same cue type used at storage is worth doing only if the rewriter is accurate. A weak rewriter adds nothing.

source: Li Ji-An, Zhou, Benna, Mattar (2024) Linking In-context Learning in Transformers to Human Episodic Memory (NeurIPS)
finding: Induction heads behave like the CMR (contextual maintenance and retrieval) model of human free recall. They show temporal contiguity and a forward-asymmetric attention profile. These heads sit in middle to late layers. Ablating the top 10% most CMR-like heads hurts in-context learning more than random ablation.
numbers: Models: GPT2, Pythia family, Qwen-7B, Mistral-7B, Llama3-8B. In-context learning score = loss at token 500 minus loss at token 50, 2000 C4 sequences of at least 512 tokens. Ablation raised the score (worse in-context learning) for most models, strongest where the baseline was good (GPT2, Qwen-7B). Fitted inverse temperature lies in the human range. Human reference: PEERS data, N=171.
limits: Authors warn of the Hydra effect (other heads compensate) and say the causal role of the CMR-like behavior itself is unproven. Free-recall order effects, not context-match effects. Pythia ablation effects were unclear.
agent_relevance: Gives a mechanism for context-dependent recall inside the model, but it is about order in the context window, not about our lesson keys. Weak design value; keep as background.

source: Gershman, Fiete, Irie (2025) Key-value memory in the brain
finding: Argues memory uses separate keys (for retrieval) and values (for storage), so forgetting is often retrieval failure, as Tulving held. Includes a toy network where a forgotten task is restored by amplifying the stored keys, with no retraining.
numbers: Two-task network (MNIST then FashionMNIST, 5 epochs each, 64 hidden units): task 1 accuracy 99% -> 9% after task 2; scaling the task 1 key-value pairs by a factor above 1 restored it without retraining.
limits: Theory paper; the authors call the links to the brain 'speculative'. The restoration is a toy demonstration in a small network, not an LLM. Direct empirical tests are still missing.
agent_relevance: Reasonable framing for a lesson store: a lesson that is stored but never retrieved is a key problem, not a content problem. Log retrieval misses separately from wrong content.

source: Berglund et al. (2024) The Reversal Curse: LLMs trained on 'A is B' fail to learn 'B is A' (ICLR) [Exp 1, fine-tuning]
finding: A parametric-memory version of cue direction. After fine-tuning on 'Name is description', the model answers 'who is <description>?' at about chance, though it answers the matching-direction question well. Paraphrase augmentation in the same direction did not fix it.
numbers: GPT-3-175B: NameToDescription prompts 50.0 +/- 2.1% same direction, 0.0 +/- 0.0% reverse; DescriptionToName 96.7 +/- 1.2% same, 0.1 +/- 0.1% reverse. 30 fictitious facts, 30 paraphrases each (900 docs per subset). Also tested Llama-1 and other sizes.
quote: models do not generalize a prevalent pattern in their training set
limits: Exact-match scoring on a small synthetic fact set. Not a test of context match in the human sense; it shows retrieval depends on the direction in which the fact was encoded.
agent_relevance: A lesson stored as 'when X, do Y' may not be found from a Y-side query. If the agent will search from a symptom, write the lesson with the symptom first.

source: Berglund et al. (2024) Reversal Curse [Exp 2, real celebrities, and in-context control]
finding: On real facts, GPT-4 answers the forward question far more often than the reverse. If 'A is B' is placed in the prompt, the model can reverse it, so the failure is in stored (parametric) retrieval, not in logic.
numbers: GPT-4: 79% for 'Who is Tom Cruise's mother?' type questions vs 33% for the reversed 'Who is Mary Lee Pfeiffer's son?' type.
limits: Authors note Exp 2 is not a direct test because the training set is unknown, and conclusions are 'somewhat tentative'. Follow-up work on how general the effect is was not read here.
agent_relevance: Putting the lesson in the prompt removes the cue problem. The cue problem lives in how the lesson is found, so spend design effort on lookup, not on how well the model reasons once it has the lesson.

source: Allen-Zhu and Li (2023) Physics of Language Models 3.1: Knowledge Storage and Extraction
finding: Models can store a fact yet fail to extract it under a different question unless the pretraining text showed the fact in varied wordings and orders. Linear probes show the fact is tied to the person's name tokens only when text was augmented. This is cue-dependent retrieval in parametric memory.
numbers: Synthetic biographies (bioS, 100,000 people). Plain biography then QA fine-tuning: low out-of-distribution extraction (33% only on birthdate, which always came first). With 5 diverse biography entries per person (rewording, sentence shuffle) QA accuracy rose from 9.7% to 96.6%. Mixed training (QA data for half of people included in pretraining) gave 86.6% (bioS) and 77.7% (bioR).
limits: Models trained from scratch on synthetic data. Real-model transfer is argued by analogy (real internet data has natural multiplicity). Not about prompts at inference.
agent_relevance: Diversity of encoding forms is the cure in parametric memory. For a lesson store, the matching move is to write several differently worded versions of a lesson or several cue sets.

source: Chauvet (2024) Memory GAPS: Would LLMs pass the Tulving Test?
finding: Runs Tulving's direct-comparison design (recognition vs recall, with copy, associated, rhyme and unrelated cues) on one 7B model. Immediate recognition is perfect, but delayed recall from the very word that was studied fails. Answers drift to pretrained associations, not the study list.
numbers: Mistral-7b-instruct-v0, 48-word list, 32 cues per run (8 per cue type), 384 observations per table. Immediate recognition: copy cues 100%, no false positives. Delayed recall with copy cues: 0 words recalled. Ordinal cues ('first word in the list'): first 4-5 answered right in immediate tests; delayed tests drew words from another list (edible fruits).
quote: a copy cue does not recall a single word of the study list, even though the cue is itself that target word!
limits: One small model, no replication across models, small cell counts. Tables in the preprint are partly garbled in text form so I cite only the clear cells. 'Delayed' means a later turn of the same chat. Single author, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: A fact placed earlier in a chat can be lost even when the exact word is the cue, and pretrained associations can take over. Re-injecting needed lessons near the question is safer than trusting recall from earlier turns.

source: Chauvet (2024) Memory Traces: Are Transformers Tulving Machines?
finding: Repeats the Tulving and Watkins (1975) trace-valence test with associative and rhyme cues at encoding and retrieval. The LLM recalls much better with associative cues than rhyme cues; humans are balanced. The method's assumption that a failed cue leaves the trace unchanged does not hold for the LLM.
numbers: Mistral-7b-instruct-v0. Both targets recalled across two cue orders after associative encoding: LLM 0.53 vs human 0.32 and 0.36 (as the paper reports). Failure to recall under any cue is higher in the LLM by .08 and .09 for the two encodings. Assumption violation (trace changed by earlier cue): discrepancy .08 (associative) and .17 (rhyme) vs .06 in the human data.
limits: One small model, chat-based encoding (the list sits in context), small N. Rhyme cues are a surface-form cue that LLMs handle badly because of tokenization, so the gap may not generalize to other surface cues.
agent_relevance: The earlier cue in a chat can change what the next cue returns. Run each lesson lookup in a fresh call, not after other lookups in the same context.

source: Huet et al. (2025) Episodic Memories Generation and Evaluation Benchmark for Large Language Models (EpBench, ICLR)
finding: Builds a benchmark from the encoding specificity idea: recall questions with cues made of time, space, entity and event content, grouped by how many events match the cue (cue overload). Even the best models fall as more events match one cue. Naive fine-tuning on the book is the worst setting for multi-event cues.
numbers: Models: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude 3 Haiku, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.1 405B, o1-mini; in-context, RAG (text-embedding-3-small over paragraphs) and fine-tuning. Questions with 0, 1, 2, 3-5, 6+ matching events (150/150/90/98/60 in the long-book recall test). Text: F1 falls for every model once 2+ events match a cue. Fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini: F1 0.83 on single-event questions, 0.37 on multi-event. GPT-4o in-context and Claude 3.5 Sonnet with RAG ranked highest with no significant difference; RAG helped only a little except for GPT-4o.
limits: Synthetic, LLM-written books (Claude 3.5 Sonnet), so entity-position shortcuts exist. The per-model table in the text I read was partly garbled, so I quote only numbers stated in prose.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM evidence that cue overload is the main limit: the more lessons that match a cue, the worse recall. Keep lesson keys narrow and keep the match count visible.

source: Gao, Ma, Lin, Callan (2023) Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels (HyDE, ACL)
finding: Instead of matching the raw question to stored text, HyDE has an LLM write a made-up answer document, embeds that, and retrieves real documents near it. This turns the query into the same form as the stored traces, a query-side cue transformation.
numbers: TREC DL19 / DL20 (mAP / nDCG@10 / recall@1k): unsupervised Contriever 24.0/44.5/74.6 and 24.0/42.1/75.4; HyDE 41.8/61.3/88.0 and 38.2/57.9/84.4; fine-tuned Contriever-FT 41.7/62.1/83.6 and 43.6/63.2/85.8. HyDE used InstructGPT.
limits: Generated text can be wrong; helps most when the corpus is in a consistent style. Gains were smaller against fine-tuned strong baselines. 2022 models (InstructGPT).
agent_relevance: If lessons are stored in a fixed template, write the lookup query in the same template first (draft the lesson you would need), then search.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior (UIST) [retrieval and ablations]
finding: Retrieval scores each memory by recency, importance and relevance (embedding cosine to the current query) and keeps the top ones that fit. Removing memory, planning and reflection steadily lowers believability. Relevance is conditioned on the current situation, which is the cue.
numbers: 100 raters; TrueSkill believability: full architecture mu=29.89, no reflection 26.88, no reflection or planning 25.64, human crowdworker 22.95, no memory/planning/reflection 21.21. Full vs prior-work baseline d=8.16. Kruskal-Wallis chi2(4)=150.29, p<0.001. The paper does not ablate the three retrieval terms separately.
limits: Believability is rated by raters on interview answers, not recall accuracy. No cue manipulation. Embeddings are generic. The score weights were all set to 1.
agent_relevance: A simple, widely copied cue-match plus recency plus importance score; shows a working baseline but gives no evidence on which term matters.

source: Xu et al. (2025) A-MEM: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents
finding: At write time the LLM adds keywords, tags and a context description to each note, links related notes, and can update old notes. This is encoding-time cue enrichment. It beat plain-history and other memory agents on LoCoMo, mostly on temporal and multi-hop questions, with much lower prompt length.
numbers: LoCoMo with GPT-4o-mini, F1: temporal 45.85 (A-MEM) vs 25.52 (MemGPT) vs 18.41 (LoCoMo baseline); multi-hop 27.02 vs 26.65 vs 25.02; single hop 44.65 vs 41.04 vs 40.36. Average prompt length 643 tokens vs 16,910 for LoCoMo or MemGPT. Ablation: removing link generation and memory evolution gave 9.65 in the first (multi-hop F1) column of the ablation table, far below the full system.
limits: Authors' own benchmark runs; on some rows (e.g. single hop with GPT-4o) the LoCoMo baseline is higher. Ablation does not remove keywords and tags alone, so the keyword contribution is not isolated.
agent_relevance: Evidence that LLM-written keywords/tags at write time are a usable memory design, but not that cues drove the gain. A clean key-only ablation would be our own test.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) A Multi-Memory Segment System for Generating High-Quality Long-Term Memory Content in Agents
finding: Builds retrieval units from keywords, short-term text, several 'cognitive perspective' rewrites and episodic summaries, citing encoding specificity. Several viewpoints per memory help when questions arrive from different angles. Adding a semantic-summary segment lowered recall because its form was far from the user's wording.
numbers: LoCoMo, GPT-4o base. Ablation averages (R@1/R@3/R@5): full MMS 29.35/40.23/46.61; single-module removals roughly 27-29/38-39/45-46; removing both cognitive-perspective and episodic units 22.49/32.94/38.99 (row labels recovered from garbled text). Authors report 8-11 point recall gains on multi-hop over A-MEM with GPT-4o and Gemini.
limits: Differences between single-module removals are about 1-2 points and no variance is given. Row alignment in the ablation table is uncertain from text extraction. Keyword benefit depends on question type (helps inferential questions, not temporal).
agent_relevance: Support for multi-view keys, with a warning: an abstract summary used as a key can sit too far from the real query wording.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (TACL)
finding: Not a cue-match test, but a position effect on use of provided evidence: accuracy is highest when the answer passage is first or last and lowest in the middle. Relevant to where a retrieved lesson is placed in the prompt.
numbers: Multi-document QA with 10, 20, 30 documents. GPT-3.5-Turbo accuracy can drop by more than 20% when the answer document is in the middle; in the worst case it falls below closed-book accuracy of 56.1%.
limits: Measured on 2023 models (GPT-3.5, Claude 1.3, MPT, LongChat). Newer long-context models may differ; not tested here. Position effect, not encoding specificity.
agent_relevance: Put retrieved lessons at the start or end of the prompt, close to the task.

source: Hu et al. (2025) Evaluating Memory in LLM Agents via Incremental Multi-Turn Interactions (MemoryAgentBench)
finding: Tests four abilities (accurate retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding, selective forgetting) with long inputs fed in pieces. RAG agents do best on accurate retrieval. Long-context models do best on learning and long-range tasks. All methods fail on multi-hop selective forgetting.
numbers: Multi-hop selective forgetting (FactConsolidation-MH, built from MQuAKE edit pairs, contexts 6K to 262K tokens): no method above 28% accuracy. RAG agents beat the GPT-4o-mini backbone on accurate retrieval tasks.
limits: No test of cue mismatch. Included to show where retrieval of single snippets works and where it breaks. Exact table numbers not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of one snippet is a solved case; stale or conflicting lessons are not. A lesson store needs a way to supersede old lessons.

source: Jiang, Xu, Araki, Neubig (2020) How Can We Know What Language Models Know? (TACL)
finding: Different wordings of the same fact query give different accuracy. Mining better prompts and paraphrasing them, then pooling answers, lifts LAMA fact recall. A parametric analogue of cue-dependent retrieval.
numbers: LAMA accuracy 31.1% -> 39.6% with mined and paraphrased prompts plus ensembling (abstract page only; per-method breakdown not seen).
limits: Only the abstract page was read, not the paper. Older BERT-class models.
agent_relevance: A single query wording underestimates what is stored. Try several phrasings of a lookup before concluding a lesson is absent.

source: Eldan and Russinovich (2023) Who's Harry Potter? Approximate Unlearning in LLMs (as cited by Dinh et al. 2026)
finding: Replacing topic keywords with generic placeholders makes the model lose its ability to recall facts about the topic. This is read as evidence that keywords act as retrieval cues in model memory.
numbers: No numbers recorded; I only saw the description in Dinh et al. (2026).
limits: Second-hand; the paper itself was not opened. The Dinh paper notes collateral damage to other abilities.
agent_relevance: Supports the keyword-as-cue idea indirectly. Do not rely on it until read in full.

source: Ryu and Lewis (2021); Timkey and Linzen (2023); Yoshida et al. (2025) transformer attention and cue-based retrieval in sentence processing (as cited by Dinh et al. 2026)
finding: Prior work compares transformer attention to cue-based retrieval models of human sentence comprehension (Van Dyke and Lewis 2003), including similarity-based interference effects.
numbers: No numbers recorded; cited descriptions only.
limits: Second-hand through one 2026 preprint; none of the cited papers were opened. These are about sentence-level syntax, not memory for episodes.
agent_relevance: Background only. The computational psycholinguistics line may offer interference tests for our key design, to be read in a later pass.

source: MemoCue and CDMem (agent memory work with cue-rich query rewriting or context-dependent indexing; seen only in a search listing)
finding: MemoCue rewrites a user query into a cue-rich query to help recall memories. CDMem uses a graph-structured, context-dependent index. Neither was read.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Search snippet only; claims and results unverified.
agent_relevance: Candidates for a later read: query-side cue enrichment in an agent loop.
